parts.problem_md:
A parcel delivery company uses a program to sort parcels. The program is built from five modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Dispatch` | • has no parameters
• calls `CountParcels` once and stores the value returned
• then calls `Weigh` once for each parcel, numbered 1 to the value returned by `CountParcels`
• after each call to `Weigh`, calls either `Express` or `Standard`, decided when the program runs
• calls `Express` when the value returned by `Weigh` is greater than 2000, otherwise calls `Standard`
• does not return a value | | `CountParcels` | • has no parameters
• returns an integer value, which is the number of parcels waiting | | `Weigh` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• returns an integer value, which is the mass of that parcel in grams | | `Express` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• does not return a value | | `Standard` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• does not return a value | Write the equivalent pseudocode for module `Dispatch`. Do not write the pseudocode for the other four modules.
parts.solution_md:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `PROCEDURE Dispatch()` with no parameters, closed with `ENDPROCEDURE`
> 
> **1 mark** for declaring the local variables with correct data types
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the value returned by `CountParcels` in a variable
> 
> **1 mark** for a loop that runs once for each parcel, from 1 to that stored value, correctly closed
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the value returned by `Weigh`, called with the parcel number, inside the loop
> 
> **1 mark** for selection inside the loop that calls `Express` when the mass is greater than 2000 and `Standard` otherwise
> 
> Accept a conditional loop in place of the count-controlled loop, provided its counter is initialised before the loop and incremented inside it, for example `WHILE ParcelNum <= Total`.
> 
> Accept `NEXT` written without the identifier.
> 
> Accept the condition written as `Mass >= 2001`, since the mass is an integer number of grams.
> 
> Accept `IF Weigh(ParcelNum) > 2000 THEN` only where `Weigh` is then not called a second time.
> 
> Do not accept `FUNCTION Dispatch()`. `Dispatch` returns no value.
> 
> Do not accept `CALL CountParcels()` or `CALL Weigh(ParcelNum)`. `CALL` introduces a procedure call, and a function call must appear on the right of an assignment so that its value is kept.
> 
> Do not accept selection placed after the loop. Every parcel is weighed and routed separately, so `ENDIF` must come before `NEXT`.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each phrase in the description maps onto one pseudocode construct. "Calls A followed by B" is sequence, "decided when the program runs" is the diamond and becomes `IF ... ELSE ... ENDIF`, and "once for each parcel" is the curved arrow and becomes `FOR ... NEXT`. Write the empty loop and the empty selection first, then drop the calls inside them.
> 
> The mark most often lost here is the nesting. If you write `NEXT ParcelNum` before `ENDIF`, the program weighs every parcel but routes only the last one. Line up each closing keyword under the keyword that opened it before you move on.
> 
> The other frequent error is `CALL` in front of a function. `Weigh` hands back a value, so it belongs on the right of an arrow: `Mass ← Weigh(ParcelNum)`. Writing `CALL Weigh(ParcelNum)` throws the mass away.

parts.problem_md:
A weather station program is built from three modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Record` | • has no parameters
• calls `ReadTemp` followed by `StoreTemp` | | `ReadTemp` | • called with parameter `SensorID`, of type integer
• returns a real value | | `StoreTemp` | • called with parameter `Saved`, of type Boolean
• `Saved` is passed by reference
• does not return a value | Write the pseudocode module headers for `ReadTemp` and `StoreTemp`.
parts.solution_md:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `FUNCTION ReadTemp(SensorID : INTEGER)`, with the parameter name and its data type
> 
> **1 mark** for `RETURNS REAL`
> 
> **1 mark** for `PROCEDURE StoreTemp(BYREF Saved : BOOLEAN)`, with `BYREF` and the data type
> 
> Accept `ENDFUNCTION` and `ENDPROCEDURE` written as well, even though only the headers were asked for.
> 
> Accept any spacing around the colon and the brackets.
> 
> Do not accept `FUNCTION StoreTemp`. `StoreTemp` returns no value, so it is a procedure.
> 
> Do not accept `BYVAL Saved`. A parameter passed by value cannot pass a change back to `Record`.
> 
> Do not accept `PROCEDURE ReadTemp`, or a header with `RETURNS` missing or with the wrong return type.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word FUNCTION or PROCEDURE is decided by one thing only: does the description say a value is returned? Students lose this mark by reasoning that `StoreTemp` "sends something back" because `Saved` is passed by reference. Passing by reference is not the same as returning a value, and a module that does it is still a procedure.
> 
> Write the return type every time. `RETURNS` on its own earns nothing, and a real value returned as `RETURNS INTEGER` is wrong even though the rest of the header is right.

parts.problem_md:
A program controls a ticket machine at a railway station. The program is built from four modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Sell` | calls `GetZone` followed by `PrintTicket` | | `GetZone` | • has no parameters
• returns an integer value | | `PrintTicket` | • called with parameter `Zone`, of type integer
• repeatedly calls `PrintLine` | | `PrintLine` | • called with parameter `Text`, of type string | (a) Identify the module that would be implemented as a function. (b) The structure chart uses a curved arrow symbol to show iteration. Identify the module that this symbol is applied to.
parts.solution_md:
(a) `GetZone` **[1]**

(b) `PrintTicket` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `GetZone` in part (a)
> 
> **1 mark** for `PrintTicket` in part (b)
> 
> Accept the module name written with or without brackets, so `GetZone()` and `PrintTicket()` are both credited.
> 
> Do not accept `PrintLine` in part (b). The iteration arrow is applied to the module that makes the repeated calls, not to the module that is called repeatedly.
> 
> Do not accept `Sell` in part (b). `Sell` calls `GetZone` and `PrintTicket` once each, in sequence, so the line from `Sell` carries no iteration arrow.
> 
> Do not accept `PrintTicket` in part (a). It returns no value, so it is a procedure.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A module is a function only when the description says it returns a value. Changing a parameter, or doing a lot of work, does not make a module a function. `PrintTicket` prints a whole ticket and is still a procedure.
> 
> The words in the description tell you which symbol the chart carries. "Repeatedly calls" gives the curved arrow, and "decided when the program runs" gives the diamond. Both symbols belong to the module doing the calling, so stay on the row where you found the words.

parts.problem_md:
An electric vehicle charging point is controlled by a program.

The behaviour of the program is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the program:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| S2 | Start-Charge | Begin-Power | S3 |
| S2 | Unplug | none | S1 |
| S3 | Stop-Charge | End-Power | S2 |
| S3 | Full-Battery | Show-Full | S4 |
| S3 | Fault-Found | Show-Error | S5 |
| S4 | Unplug | Show-Total | S1 |
| S5 | Reset | none | S1 |

One driver uses the charging point. Complete the table below to show the inputs, outputs and next states.

Assume that the current state for each row is given by the Next state on the previous row. For example, the first Plug-In is made when the program is in state S1.

If there is no output for a given transition, the output cell should contain none.

The first two rows have been completed.

| Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | S1 |
| Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| Start-Charge |   |   |
|   | End-Power |   |
|   |   | S3 |
| Full-Battery |   |   |
|   |   | S1 |
parts.solution_md:
| Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | S1 |
| Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| Start-Charge | **Begin-Power** | **S3** |
| **Stop-Charge** | End-Power | **S2** |
| **Start-Charge** | **Begin-Power** | S3 |
| Full-Battery | **Show-Full** | **S4** |
| **Unplug** | **Show-Total** | S1 |

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark per row, for rows 3 to 7. Every cell in a row must be correct for that row to earn its mark.
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: Start-Charge, Begin-Power, S3
> 
> **1 mark** for row 4: Stop-Charge, End-Power, S2
> 
> **1 mark** for row 5: Start-Charge, Begin-Power, S3
> 
> **1 mark** for row 6: Full-Battery, Show-Full, S4
> 
> **1 mark** for row 7: Unplug, Show-Total, S1
> 
> Do not accept Full-Battery in row 4. Full-Battery is also an input from S3, but its output is Show-Full, not End-Power
> 
> Do not accept Unplug in row 5. Unplug is an input from S2, but it gives an output of none and a next state of S1, which does not match the S3 already given
> 
> Do not accept Reset in row 7. Reset is an input from S5, and the program is in S4 at the start of row 7

> **[exam-tip]**
> The current state is never written in this table, so you must keep track of it yourself. Before filling a row, look at the Next state in the row above and use that as the current state. Write it in the margin if it helps.
> 
> Rows 4, 5 and 7 are the hard ones because you are given the wrong end of the transition and must work backwards. For row 4 the current state is S3 and the output is End-Power, so find the row of the first table that starts at S3 and outputs End-Power. Students who instead read down the first table in order and copy the next input they see will get row 4 wrong, and then every row after it, because one wrong next state carries all the way down.

parts.problem_md:
The entry gate of a car park is controlled by a program. A driver presses a button to receive a ticket, and the gate opens when the ticket is taken.

The behaviour of the program is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the program:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Press-Button | Print-Ticket | S2 |
| S2 | Take-Ticket | Open-Gate | S3 |
| S2 | Timeout | none | S1 |
| S3 | Car-Detected | none | S4 |
| S3 | Timeout | Close-Gate | S1 |
| S4 | Car-Gone | Close-Gate | S1 |
| S4 | Timeout | Sound-Alarm | S5 |

The current state is S1. The following inputs occur, in this order:

1. Press-Button
2. Take-Ticket
3. Timeout
4. Press-Button
5. Timeout

Give the number of outputs that are produced, the outputs in the order they are produced, and the current state after the last input.
parts.solution_md:
Number of outputs: 4 **[1]**

Outputs in order: Print-Ticket, Open-Gate, Close-Gate, Print-Ticket **[1]**

Current state: S1 **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the number of outputs given as 4
> 
> **1 mark** for the four outputs listed in this exact order: Print-Ticket, Open-Gate, Close-Gate, Print-Ticket
> 
> **1 mark** for the current state given as S1
> 
> Accept "four" written in words.
> 
> Accept the outputs separated by commas, by arrows or written on separate lines, provided the order is correct.
> 
> Do not accept 5 for the number of outputs. The fifth input, Timeout from S2, has an output of none, so it produces no output.
> 
> Do not accept S2 as the current state. S2 is the state reached after the fourth input, not after the fifth.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work one input at a time and write the state down after each one. The most common mistake here is counting an output of none as an output, which gives 5 instead of 4. A row with none in the Output column still changes the state, it just produces nothing.
> 
> The second most common mistake is stopping one input early. There are five inputs, so trace all five. The state you must give is the one reached after input 5, even though input 5 produces no output.

parts.problem_md:
A company installs parcel collection lockers in shops. A customer collects a parcel by scanning a code at the locker.

The behaviour of the locker software is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the software:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Scan-Code | Show-Menu | S2 |
| S2 | Press-Open | Open-Door | S3 |
| S2 | Press-Cancel | none | S1 |
| S2 | Scan-Code | Show-Error | S2 |
| S3 | Close-Door | Lock-Door | S1 |
| S3 | Timeout | Show-Alert | S4 |

Complete the table with reference to the information above.

|   | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of different inputs |   |
| The final or halting state |   |
parts.solution_md:
|   | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of different inputs | **5** |
| The final or halting state | **S4** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the number of different inputs given as 5
> 
> **1 mark** for the final or halting state given as S4
> 
> Accept "five" written in words for the first row
> 
> Do not accept 6 for the first row. There are six transitions, but Scan-Code appears twice, so only five different input values are used
> 
> Do not accept S1 for the second row. S1 is where the software starts, not where it stops

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "different" is doing the work in the first row. Count the distinct values in the Input column, not the number of rows. Here Scan-Code is used twice, once from S1 and once from S2, so six transitions use only five different inputs.
> 
> To find the halting state, look for a state that appears in the Next state column but never in the Current state column. Once the software reaches S4 there is no row that can take it anywhere else, so it stops there.

parts.problem_md:
Seven program modules form part of a program. A description of the relationship between the modules is summarised below. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | Mod-A | calls Mod-B followed by Mod-C | | Mod-B | • called with parameters Par1 and Par2
• calls either Mod-D or Mod-E, determined when the program runs
• returns a Boolean value | | Mod-C | • called with parameters Par1 and Par3
• Par3 is passed by reference
• repeatedly calls Mod-F followed by Mod-G | | Mod-D | called with parameter Par2 | | Mod-E | • called with parameter Par3
• returns an integer value | | Mod-F | called with parameter Par3 | | Mod-G | • called with parameter Par3
• Par3 is passed by reference | Parameters in the table are as follows: - Par1 and Par3 are of type string. - Par2 is of type integer. Draw a structure chart to show the relationship between the seven modules and the parameters passed between them.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> ![Flowchart illustrating module interactions: Mod-A at top, branching to Mod-B and Mod-C, leading to Mod-D, Mod-E, Mod-F, and Mod-G with arrows and parameters.](assets/001-flowchart-illustrating-module-interactions-mod-a.png)
> 
> One mark per bullet:
> 
> 1. All modules correctly labelled and interconnected
> 2. Parameters between Mod-A and Mod-B and return value from Mod-B
> 3. Parameters between Mod-A and Mod-C

parts.problem_md:
A teacher is designing a program to process pseudocode projects written by her students.

Each student project is stored in a text file.

The process is split into a number of stages. Each stage performs a different task and creates a new file.

For example:

| File name | Comment |
|---|---|
| `MichaelAday_src.txt` | Student project file produced by student Michael Aday |
| `MichaelAday_S1.txt` | File produced by stage 1 |
| `MichaelAday_S2.txt` | File produced by stage 2 |

Suggest a reason why the teacher’s program has been split into a number of stages **and **give the benefit of producing a different file from each stage.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark for reason, one for benefit
> 
> Reason: (Program is) easier to design / implement / test / debug / modify
> 
> Benefit: Easier to check that **each stage** works as expected

parts.problem_md:

The system stores information for each club member: name, home address, email address, mobile phone number, date of birth and exercise preferences.

Many classes are full, and the club creates a waiting list for each class. The club adds details of members who want to join a class that is full to the waiting list for that class.

When the system identifies that a space is available in one of the classes, a new module will send a text message to each member who is on the waiting list.

A different part of the program is represented by the following state‑transition diagram.

(i) Complete the table to show the inputs, outputs and next states.

Assume that the current state for each row is given by the ‘Next state’ on the previous row. For example, the first Input‑A is made when in state S1.

If there is no output for a given transition, then the output cell should contain ‘none’.

The first two rows have been completed.

| Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | S1 |
| Input‑A | none | S3 |
|   | Output‑W |   |
|   | none |   |
| Input‑B |   |   |
| Input‑A |   |   |
|   |   | S4 |

(5)

(ii) Identify the input sequence that will cause the minimum number of state changes in the transition from S1 to S4.

(1)
parts.solution_md:

> (i)
> 
> | Input | Output | Next state |
> |---|---|---|

parts.problem_md:
A fitness club has a computerised membership system. The fitness club offers a number of different exercise classes.

The following information is stored for each club member: name, home address, email address, mobile phone number, date of birth and the exercise(s) they are interested in.

The structure chart illustrates part of the membership program:

![Flowchart with decision diamond labelled "Update," arrows to boxes "Sub-A," "Sub-B," and "Sub-C," with annotations "Name," "P1," "P2," and "T1."](assets/003-flowchart-with-decision-diamond-labelled-update-.png)

Data item notes:

- Name contains the name of a club member
- P1 and T1 are of type real.

Explain the meaning of the diamond symbol (labelled with the letter A) in the chart.
parts.solution_md:

> Means that `Update `calls (one of) either `Sub-A`, `Sub-B `or `Sub-C `
> 
> One mark for each point:

> - naming all four modules correctly

parts.problem_md:
A coffee shop owner wants to introduce a computerised loyalty card system.

A programmer discusses the details of the system with the shop owner.

The shop will give each customer a loyalty card that displays a unique customer ID as a bar code. A customer will be able to present their card each time they make a purchase. The system will scan the bar code, calculate points, and add them to the customer’s total. When the customer next makes a purchase and presents their card, they will have the option to exchange points for a discount.

The designer decides that this activity will be handled by a new module. Decomposition will be used to break the problem of designing the new module down into sub-problems (sub-modules).

Identify **four **sub-modules that could be used in the design of the new module and describe their use.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark for name **and **use
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> Examples include:
> 
> Sub-module: `ScanCard()/ GetID() `
> Use: Read the barcode from the loyalty card / Get the customer ID from the barcode
> 
> Sub-module: `GetPoints() `
> Use: Get the number of points the customer has
> 
> Sub-module:` ExchangePoints() / UpdateCard() `
> Use: Reduce the number of loyalty points
> 
> Sub-module: `GetDiscount() / CalculateDiscount() `
> Use: Calculate the discount
> 
> Sub-module: `CalculatePoints() `
> Use: Calculate points (following a purchase)
> 
> Sub-module: `UpdatePoints() `
> Use: Update total points a customer has (following a purchase)
> 
> Sub-module: `ShowDiscount() `
> Use: Display the discount
> 
> **Max 4 marks**

parts.problem_md:
A coffee shop runs a computerised loyalty card system.

Customers are issued with a loyalty card with their name together with a unique customer ID.

Loyalty points are added to their card each time they spend money at the shop.

The following information is stored for each customer: ID, name, home address, email address, mobile phone number, date of birth, number of points, date of last visit and amount of money spent at last visit.

A new module will generate a personalised email message to each loyalty card customer who has not visited the coffee shop in the last three months. The message will include a unique voucher code which can be used to authorise a discount if the customer goes to the shop within the next two weeks.

It is decided to adopt a formal program development life cycle model for the development of the new module.

The analysis of the new module is complete and the project moves on to the design stage. During this stage all the necessary algorithms and module designs will be defined.

State **three other** items that will be defined for the new module during the design stage.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **MP1 **Data structures // data dictionary // identifier table(s) // validation rules
> 
> **MP2** Data-flow diagram // state-transition diagram
> 
> **MP3 **User interface // Format for the email
> 
> **MP4 **Testing method / Test plan / Test data / Trace tables
> 
> **MP5** Choice of email protocol to be used // Programming language to be used // Development environment
> 
> **MP6 **Use of library routines // program to send the email
> 
> **Max 3 marks**

Module `Connect() `will call either `Activate() `or `Sync()`. This is decided at run-time.

Complete the structure chart for these modules.

parts.problem_md:
A program includes the following assignment statement:

`Result ← STR_TO_NUM(x) / STR_TO_NUM(y) `

When the program evaluates the expression in the statement, it performs a calculation.

Variable `Result `is of type real and variables `x` and `y` are of type string.

Two checks are required before the calculation is performed:

1. The two strings represent valid numeric values.
2. The numeric value of string `y` is not zero.

The designer considers implementing the** checks and calculation **as a module (a procedure or a function). One reason for this is that the same checks and calculations are performed at several places in the program.

Give **another **reason why this is a suitable approach **and **state what is avoided by this approach.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers include:
> 
> **Reason: **
> 
> - This part of the algorithm performs a specific task // if the check or calculation is changed it is changed only once
> - A (similar) subroutine is already available // Library routine is already available
> - The program is simplified / easier to understand / easier to design / code / test / debug / maintain
> 
> **Max 1 marks for 'Reason' **
> 
> **Avoided: **
> 
> - Unnecessary code duplication
> - Errors caused by differences where several copies of the check and calculation exist
> 
> **Max 1 marks for 'Avoided'**

parts.problem_md:
An algorithm is represented by a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the algorithm:

| **Current state** | **Input** | **Output** | **Next state** |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | A1 | X1 | S2 |
| S2 | A3 | none | S1 |
| S2 | A2 | X4 | S5 |
| S5 | A1 | X1 | S5 |
| S5 | A4 | X2 | S2 |
| S5 | A3 | none | S3 |
| S1 | A9 | X9 | S3 |
| S3 | A9 | X9 | S4 |

Complete the state-transition diagram to represent the information given in the table.

![Flowchart with two circles, one labelled S1 and the other unlabelled, arrows indicate transitions with labels A1|X1, A3; a start point leads to S1.](assets/007-flowchart-with-two-circles-one-labelled-s1-and-t.png)
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> ![Flowchart depicting a state machine with five states (S1 to S5), arrows showing transitions, and labels for conditions and actions like A1|X1.](assets/008-flowchart-depicting-a-state-machine-with-five-st.png)
